transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um, hi. Yeah, I'm here because... well, I keep having these nights where I just eat an amount of food that honestly scares me. Like, I’ll start with some leftovers after I sit down to grade papers. I teach fourth grade, and right now we're doing fractions, which is just... it's a nightmare to grade because half the kids don't show their work. One of my students, Leo, he actually wrote a whole paragraph on why fractions are useless instead of solving the problem. It was funny, but, you know, I still had to mark it wrong. 

But anyway, where was I? Oh, so I'll be grading, and I'll finish my leftovers, and then I just... I can't stop. I'll go through a whole box of cereal, then crackers, half a jar of peanut butter... I even end up eating the snacks I packed for my classroom. Which makes me feel terrible because I buy those with my own money. The school budget is practically nonexistent this year, and if I don't give the kids a snack before recess, they get so cranky and rowdy. But yeah, I just... I end up going through all of it myself in one sitting.
When you're eating all of that food in one sitting, do you feel like you can't stop or control what you're doing?

Yeah, exactly. It's like... once I start, it feels like the reasonable, put-together teacher part of me is just hovering there, watching from the outside and saying, "Joan, stop." But my hands just have a mind of their own. They keep opening wrappers and jars and putting food in my mouth until I'm so painfully full I can barely breathe. 

It's actually a lot like how my student, Sarah, acts when she gets into the art supplies. I swear, that girl cannot control herself around glitter. Just last Tuesday, I turned my back for two seconds to help another student with their spelling worksheet—we were doing words with silent E's, which is always a struggle for them—and by the time I turned around, Sarah had dumped an entire tube of green glitter all over the reading rug. The custodian, Mr. Henderson, was so mad at me. He’s retiring next month and he’s just completely checked out, you know? He told me he’s moving to Florida to live near his daughter, which sounds nice, honestly, with how cold it's been getting here. I hate the winter. 

But anyway... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, my hands. Yeah, I just can't stop myself once I start eating.
Do you find yourself eating much more rapidly than normal during these episodes, and do you usually eat until you feel uncomfortably full?

Um, I don't really know about how fast I'm going. I haven't really noticed if it's more rapid than normal. I mean, I'm so used to eating fast anyway just because of my job. We literally get twenty-two minutes for lunch, and half of that is spent walking the kids down to the cafeteria and getting them settled. 

Just yesterday, I had to spend ten minutes helping this one kid, Mason, look for his lunchbox. It was this brand new Spider-Man one, and his mom is... well, she's very intense. She's the head of the PTA and she emails me constantly. Like, last week she sent me this huge, long email complaining that the classroom is too drafty for Mason. And it's like, I can't control the HVAC system! The building was built in the sixties, and the windows barely even shut all the way. I actually had to put duct tape around the frame of one of them back in November just to keep the wind out. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, rushing. Yeah, so I'm just used to rushing through my meals during the day. But at night, when I'm doing all that eating? I really couldn't tell you if I'm doing it fast. I just kind of zone out. I know I get painfully full, like I mentioned, but the actual speed of it... I'm really not sure.
Do these eating episodes cause you a lot of distress, or do they interfere with your daily life in any way?

Yeah, it... it really does. I mean, my whole life outside of school feels like it's just revolving around this. My evenings and weekends are completely planned around trying to undo what happened with the food. It's exhausting. And because of it, I've been so much slower with my grading. Which is bad, because report cards are due next Friday, and the principal, Mrs. Gable, is a stickler for deadlines. She actually called a staff meeting last week just to remind us about the deadline, and she brought these terrible store-bought muffins that were so dry. I think she got them from that discount grocery store down the street, the one where the shopping carts always have a wobbly wheel. I went there once to buy dry erase markers because the school ran out—can you believe that? We ran out of markers in October! I had to buy a whole pack of the colorful ones, and of course, the kids fought over who got to use the purple one. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, so I'm behind on grading. And I'm just less present with my friends, too. I keep canceling on them because I'm just so focused on... well, fixing things after I eat. And when I am at work, I'm just constantly worried about seeming put-together, you know? Like, what if they can tell? What if Mrs. Gable looks at me and just knows? It's really stressful.
Do you find yourself eating large amounts of food even when you’re not physically hungry?

Um, I'm not really sure about that. I guess I haven't paid that much attention to whether my stomach is actually growling or not before I start. It's more of a mental thing, I think? Like, I just need to eat. 

It kind of reminds me of how my dog, Buster, acts. He's a golden retriever mix, and I swear, that dog will eat anything at any time, hungry or not. Just last weekend, I was trying to repot some of my houseplants because they were getting totally rootbound—especially this one pothos I've had since college, it's survived three moves and a roommate who kept forgetting to water it. Anyway, I had a bag of potting soil open on the patio, and Buster just started eating it! Like, literal dirt. I had to pry his mouth open and scoop it out with my hands. It was so gross. And then, of course, I had to call the emergency vet, and the receptionist there was so unhelpful. She put me on hold for like fifteen minutes, and they play this awful elevator music that just loops the same four bars over and over. I don't understand why places can't just have normal music on hold. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being hungry. Yeah, I honestly don't know if I'm physically hungry when it happens. I just kind of do it.
After these episodes of eating a lot, do you ever try to compensate by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, exercising excessively, or doing something else to try to 'undo' the food you ate?

Um, yeah, I definitely try to undo it. I don't... I don't make myself throw up or take pills or anything like that, but I'll tell myself I'm just not allowed to eat breakfast or lunch at school the next day. Which is actually really hard because the kids always want to share their snacks. This one little girl, Chloe, she always brings these homemade granola bars that her dad makes. He's a chef at this new farm-to-table restaurant downtown, the one that used to be an old firehouse? They kept the original brick and the big bay doors, it's really cool. I went there for my friend Sarah's birthday last month, but the service was terrible. Our waiter kept disappearing, and it took them like forty-five minutes just to bring us our drinks. I ordered a mocktail that was supposed to have muddled blackberries, but I swear it just tasted like flavored syrup. 

But anyway, yeah, I won't eat during the day. And then after school, I'll go out on the trail and just run or walk for hours, or I'll do all this extra yoga. Even when I'm completely shaky and exhausted, I just force myself to keep going because I feel like I have to burn off everything from the night before.

No evidence for purging behaviors or other features of bulimia nervosa (F50.2) or unspecified eating disorder (F50.9) remains, as the clinical picture is now consistent with F50.81.
